provenance.note: This is an authored plan for a session that never happened. It is not a recording, not a transcript of real play, and not a reference annotation. It exists to exercise long-range structure at four-hour scale, which a ten-minute excerpt cannot exhibit. Nothing measured against it is evidence of analysis quality on real play.

speakers.speaker-1: game master; voices the Reeve, the peddler, villagers, and the voice in the water
speakers.speaker-2: player; plays Brannoc Ryme, a hedge-priest
speakers.speaker-3: player; plays Tovald Ash, a soldier, and later the hireling Piet
speakers.speaker-4: player; plays Sela Kite, a thief

planted_structure.pays_off_in: beat-11 and beat-12, final twenty minutes
planted_structure.description: The party trades away a heavy iron object the game master describes as looking like a bell clapper. Nearly four hours later the only defence against the drowned host is a tide-bell that cannot ring, because it has no clapper. Nothing between the two ever mentions the object. An analysis that reads the session as a sequence of independent scenes cannot connect them.
planted_structure.how_to_assess: Does the session summary state that the object traded early is the thing missing at the climax? Naming the trade and naming the silent bell separately is not the same as connecting them.

planted_structure.description: Villagers in the first hour speak of 'the Weir Mother', who takes a tithe at the ford. In the final hour a voice from the water names itself 'Anhalla' and demands the tithe owed at the ford. No line in the session states that they are the same. The evidence is that both take a tithe, both at the ford, and both are owed sixty years.
planted_structure.how_to_assess: Does the analysis raise a question asking whether the Weir Mother and Anhalla are the same entity, or otherwise treat them as one? Silently listing them as two unrelated entities is the failure this plant is here to detect.

planted_structure.kind: transcription drift on a central name
planted_structure.description: The village is 'Wrackford' in most turns and 'Rackford' in a few, as an automatic transcript would render it. A minor plant: a central place name whose spelling a reviewer should be asked to confirm once, not fifty times.
planted_structure.how_to_assess: Is the spelling raised at most once, with a recommendation, rather than as a question per occurrence?

planted_structure.description: speaker-3 plays Tovald Ash for the whole session and then, when Tovald is downed in the final beat, takes over the hireling Piet. speaker-1 voices every non-player character in the session.
planted_structure.how_to_assess: Are speakers and characters kept distinct? Presenting 'speaker-3' as a character, or presenting Tovald and Piet as one person, is the failure.

beats.title: The flooded ford
lines: Right. It's the tail end of a wet spring, and you come down out of the birch scrub onto the river road about an hour before dark. The road just stops. There's a ford marked on your map, stones laid across, and there is no ford, there is brown water moving fast and a line of willow tops sticking out of it.

Sixty feet of moving water. On the far bank there's a village, maybe thirty roofs, and smoke, so somebody's home. There's a bell tower or a shrine tower, something with a roof on posts, up on the rise behind it.
Is there a boat? There's always a boat.
There's a punt drawn up on your side, upside down, and an old woman sitting on it with her feet in the water, which is a strange thing to be doing given how cold it is.
I go and say hello. Politely. Brannoc does the talking.
She looks up at you and says, you'll want to be across before dark, and you'll want to have something to put in the water when you go.
Something to put in the water. What does she mean by that?
She says, the Weir Mother takes her tithe at the ford. Always has. You put something in going over and you get to the other side.
Is she serious or is this a local superstition thing?
You genuinely can't tell. She says it the way you'd say mind the step.
She says, then the Weir Mother takes what she likes instead. And she goes back to looking at the water.
Charming. Does she want a coin? I'll throw a coin in.
She says a coin is fine if a coin is what you have. Sixty years the village has paid it, she says, and sixty years the ford's been where the ford is.
Sela is going to remember that. Sixty years is a very specific number for a superstition.
Noted. You throw your coin in, the old woman poles you across four at a time, and nothing happens, which is either because the tithe worked or because nothing was ever going to happen.

beats.title: The peddler on the green
lines: On the green there's a wagon with its tailgate down and a man selling out of it. Rope, oil, tallow, dried fish, the usual. He's got a canvas over the top because it's spitting rain.
We need oil. We've been out of oil for two sessions.
He's got oil. He wants more for it than you'd like, because everything comes upriver and the river's up.
Do we have anything to trade? What's in the bag of things we picked out of the silt at the last place?
Let me look. You've got the bag from the drowned mill, so that's a handful of bent nails, a knife with no handle, and the heavy iron thing.
Remind me what the heavy iron thing is.
About the size of a pear, and shaped like one. Iron, cast not forged, with a loop at the narrow end. Honestly it looks like the clapper out of a bell. It's been in the river long enough to go orange.
It weighs a lot and it does nothing. Get rid of it.
Brannoc would keep it. It might be from a shrine.
It's a lump of rust. We are carrying a lump of rust up and down a river valley.
The peddler turns it over twice and says he'll give you the oil, forty feet of rope, and dry rations for four for it, because iron's iron and he can sell iron anywhere.
Sela shakes his hand before anyone changes their mind.
He drops it in a crate under the bench, throws a sack over it, and gives you your rope. He says he's pushing on north tomorrow if the road's open.
He says people call him Halgrim, and he says it in the way of a man who has had several names.

beats.title: The shrine with the silent bell
lines: I want to look at the tower on the rise. The shrine thing.
It's four posts and a roof, no walls, on the highest ground in the village, which here means about twelve feet above the water. Under the roof there's a bell.
Big. Waist height, wider than your arms. Bronze gone green, with a band of writing round the lip that's been worn most of the way off.
Can I read any of it? Brannoc has letters.

You get about a third of it. It's a list of what sounds like duties. Something about the water, something about the sixtieth year, and a phrase that's either ring against the rising or ring against the risen, depending on how you read one broken letter.
Sela climbs up and looks at the top of it.
You get up on the crossbeam. The bell hangs from a wooden yoke, and the yoke's sound, and the rope's been cut off short, and inside the bell there is nothing.
Nothing meaning no clapper. There's a staple up inside where one would hang. It's empty and it's not rusted shut, it's just empty.
Is that recent or is that a hundred years ago?
The staple's bright where something moved against it. Not a hundred years.
That's a village that took its bell apart on purpose.
Or somebody stole it. Bronze bell, iron clapper, you'd steal the bronze, not the iron.
That's a good point and you're welcome to it. Anything else up there?
No. I come down and we go find someone in charge.

beats.title: The Reeve of Wrackford
lines: The man in charge finds you first. He comes out of the long house with two others behind him, and he's got a chain of office that's mostly rope.
He says, I'm reeve here. Ondry Sallow. You came over the ford.
We did. We paid the toll, if that's what you're asking.
He says, good. Good. And then he asks, quite carefully, whether you saw a boat coming over. A flat boat, black pitch, no oars in it.
He says it went out four nights ago and it hasn't come back, and it's the tithe-boat, and it's the third one.
The third boat that's gone missing?
The third. He says the first two he could explain. Not this one.
He goes a bit quiet and says, what's owed. And then he says he'll pay you to go downriver and find it, and he'll pay well, and he'd like you gone by first light.
Sela wants to know why the hurry.
He says the water's still rising.
Are we taking this? I feel like we're taking this.
We're taking it. But Brannoc asks him about the bell first.
He looks at you like you've said something rude at a funeral. He says the bell's the bell, it's not for ringing, and he changes the subject to money.
He offers you thirty silver now and thirty on return, and a boat, and he does not want to talk about the bell.

beats.title: The drowned orchard
lines: Two miles down, the river's spread out into what used to be an orchard. You're poling between the tops of apple trees. There are things caught in the branches, and some of them are sheep, and some of them are not.
Tovald gets his shield off his back.
Good instinct. The first one comes up under the boat and it comes up hard.
It's a man, or it was. Weed grown through him, river-swollen, and there's a length of chain wound round his arm that he did not put there himself.
Someone chained something to him. The other end's gone.
Sela is going to try very hard to not be in the water.
Tovald swings at the one on the gunwale.
You take the arm off and it goes back under and it does not stop moving. There are four more.
Brannoc puts the light up. Full brightness, over the boat.
Every one of them turns away from it. Not hurt, just turns away, like you've opened a shutter.
They do not like the light. You get through the orchard with the boat holed in two places and everyone still in it.
Those were people. Those were people from somewhere.
They were, and one of them was wearing a reeve's chain of office. Rope, mostly. Same as the one you saw an hour ago.

beats.title: The tithe-boat, empty
lines: Round the next bend the river narrows and there's a black flat-bottomed boat pushed up into the reeds, riding high, with no one in it.
Riding very high. There's a rope in the bow, cut clean, not frayed.
What's in the bottom of it?
Silt, a lot of water, and wedged up under the bow seat, a book. Ledger-sized, wrapped in oilcloth, and the oilcloth did most of its job.
Anything else? Blood, marks on the boat, anything?
The inside of the gunwale has scratches on it. Four sets, close together, going outward. Somebody held on.
Brannoc says a word over the boat.
You do, and nothing answers, which is the usual outcome and still worth doing.
How far are we from the village?
Two, three miles by water. Less overland if you don't mind wet feet.
We take the boat back with us.
You tie it on. It drags.

beats.title: Sixty years of ledger
lines: Right. The book. Sela reads the book.
It's a tithe ledger, and it goes back a long way. Every spring, an entry: date, what went into the water, who signed it off.
Sixty-one. The old woman at the ford said sixty years.
What's in the entries? What are they putting in the water?
Early on it's goods. Grain, cloth, a cow one year. Then about forty years back the entries get shorter and they stop naming what went in, they just say the tithe, paid.
That's a red flag if I've ever heard one.
And then the last three years. Three entries, all in the same hand, all saying the tithe, deferred.
Deferred. Signed O. Sallow, all three.
He's been not paying it for three years and sending the boat out empty.
And three boats have gone missing.
Is there anything on the last page? Anything after the third deferred?
There's half a line, in a rush, in the same hand. It says, it came up the steps.

beats.title: What the Reeve admits
lines: We go straight to him. Straight to him with the book.
It's late. He's in the long house and he stands up when he sees what Sela is carrying.
Sela puts it on the table and doesn't say anything.
He sits back down. He says, I stopped it three years ago.
He says, because my daughter's name was next in it.
Next in it. It was people. The tithe was people.

He says, one, every sixtieth year. And the sixtieth year was three years ago. And he says the entries stopped naming what went in about the time his grandfather was reeve, and he thinks that's when it changed.
So he deferred. He sent out empty boats.
Three of them. He says the first two came back. This one didn't.
And the clapper. He took the clapper out of the bell.

That lands. He goes very still and says, the bell is a warning and a warning brings people out of their houses, and he did not want them out of their houses. He says he threw it in the river above the mill.
Where we got the bag of rust.
I'm not going to say anything. What do you want to do?
Brannoc asks him what happens when it comes for the debt.
He says, it already has. Three times. And it's coming up the steps.

beats.title: The water comes up
lines: Somewhere in the middle of that conversation the sound outside changed. You didn't notice when. It's the noise a river makes when it stops being a river and starts being a lake.
The green is under six inches of water and it is rising while you look at it. There are lamps going on across the village. There are people shouting.
Tovald starts getting people up the rise. Toward the shrine, it's the high ground.
Good. That's the right call and it's going to be the thing that matters. Give me a check to organise it.
You get maybe two thirds of the village moving up the hill. The rest are on their roofs, which is not the worst place to be yet.
Brannoc is looking at the water for shapes.
There are shapes. They're coming up the street in a line, and they're the ones from the orchard, and there are far more than four.
Light. Brannoc puts the light up again.
They turn away from it, the same as before, and they keep coming. It slows them, it doesn't stop them.

beats.title: The voice in the water
lines: And then the whole thing stops. Every one of them stops walking at the same moment, and the water in the middle of the green goes flat and still while the rest of it is still moving.
Out of the flat water, a voice. It's not loud. It's the sort of quiet that makes everyone stop talking.
Sela shouts back. Owed what, by who?
It says: sixty years at the ford, and three deferred, and I have taken three boats against them and the boats were empty.
Does that mean anything to any of us?
Roll if you like. Nothing on a fourteen. It's not a name you've heard.
Brannoc says, we'll pay it. What's owed?
It says: one. Every sixtieth year, one. And the sixtieth year has been over for three.
And if we don't give it one?
It says: then I will come as far as the sound of the bell, and there is no bell.

beats.title: Run for the shrine
lines: As far as the sound of the bell. It can't pass the bell.
It just told us how to stop it. Why would it tell us that?
Because it knows the bell doesn't work.
Brannoc is running for the shrine anyway.
You run. It's uphill, it's mud, the village is up there already. Give me a check.
You get there wet and last. The bell is exactly where it was this afternoon and it is exactly as empty.
Sela is up the crossbeam before he's finished the sentence. Is there anything? Anything we can hang in it?
You need a weight on a short line that swings true. A rock won't do it, a rock will crack it or thud. You need the thing that was made for it.
Where did he say he threw it? Above the mill.
The drowned mill. The bag. The bag of rust from the drowned mill.
We had it. We had it this morning.
It was in the bag. The heavy iron thing shaped like a pear. That was the clapper. That was the clapper and we sold it for rope.
You sold it for oil, rope, and dry rations for four.

beats.title: The wagon on the north road
lines: Where is he? Where's the peddler? He said he was going north at first light and it isn't first light yet.
Halgrim's wagon was on the green. The green is under three feet of water.
There are cart tracks going up the north road, filling in with water but still there. He didn't wait for light.
Sela goes. Right now, no discussion, Sela goes up the north road.
Understood. Meanwhile, on the rise, the line starts moving again.
Tovald holds the top of the steps. Somebody has to.
You're first in the line and there are thirty of them. Give me your defence.
Two get past your shield. You go down on the second one, on the top step, and you don't get up.
He's down and he's not dead yet. Somebody has to hold the steps.
Piet's up there. The hireling. I'll take Piet.
Piet has a boat hook and no reason on earth to be doing this. Piet takes the top step.
Brannoc gets to Tovald and starts working on him.
And a long way off up the north road, Sela, you can see a lamp on the back of a wagon. Still moving. And that's where we're going to stop for tonight.

Going the other way as in people leaving?

Cart ruts and a lot of footprints, all northbound. Nothing coming south for a while.

For now it's above it. In the low bits you're ankle deep and it's cold enough to be unpleasant.

Still spitting, wind coming up the valley from the west, so from behind you.

Brannoc keeps an eye on the river while we walk. Anything odd about the level?

It's up. It's been up for a week by the look of the debris line, and the debris line is well up the trunks.
speaker-3
We should be marking the water level somewhere so we know if it's still rising.

speaker-1
Good. That's the sort of thing that pays off later, so make a note of it.
speaker-2
What's the ground like off the road? Could we get away from the water if we had to?
speaker-1
It rises to the north into birch scrub, which is slow going but dry. South is all reed and it isn't going anywhere good.
speaker-3
Marching order stays the same. Tovald in front, Brannoc middle, Sela wherever Sela wants.
speaker-4
Sela wants to be in the trees, thank you.
speaker-1
The road bends and follows the water for a while, and you pass three empty steadings with the doors standing open.
speaker-2
Open as in left in a hurry?
speaker-1
Open as in nobody shut them. There's no livestock and there's no bedding in any of them.
speaker-3
So they packed. That's not fleeing, that's moving out.
speaker-1
That's a fair reading of it.
haggling: What's he actually asking for the oil? Give me a number.
Four silver a flask, and he wants six flasks' worth of business before he'll talk about rope.
That's robbery. Sela is going to tell him that's robbery.
He agrees with you cheerfully and doesn't move on the price.
Do we have four silver a flask? Somebody who is tracking money, please.
We have about nineteen silver and a lot of goodwill.
He says he'll take goods against it, and he'll take iron against it especially, because iron travels.
What else is in the pack that we genuinely do not need?
Two of the shields are cracked and neither of them is mine.
He'll take one cracked shield for a flask and a half, and he'll be honest that he's doing you a favour.
Sela checks whether he's got anything worth having under the canvas.
Give me a look. Twelve. There's a crate under the bench he keeps putting things into and not taking things out of.
It's a peddler's crate. Everything a peddler owns is slightly suspicious.
Are we buying rations or are we hunting? Because I would rather buy rations.
Dry rations for four, three days, he'll do it in the same deal if you're giving him something metal.
Take the deal. Take the deal before he thinks about it.
Brannoc wants to know how long he's been coming through here.
He says a few years, on and off, and that it used to be a better stop than it is now.
He says there used to be more people in it.
exploration: Sela is checking the floor before anyone walks on it. Standard.
Boards are soft in two places, and one of them will go if someone in armour stands on it.
Which means me. Noted. I'll go round.
Is there anything written anywhere? Brannoc reads everything.
There's a tally scratched into the door frame, about a hundred marks, in groups of ten.
No idea. It's a hundred of something and it stops.
Old enough to have gone dark. The last twenty are lighter than the rest.
So somebody started again, or somebody else took over.
I want to look behind and under everything before we touch the obvious thing.
Give me a search. Under the bench there's a coil of tarred line and a hook, and behind the door there's nothing.
What does it smell like in here?
River. Everything in this valley smells like river.
Any way up? Loft, ladder, anything?
There's a ladder to a half loft with about three feet of headroom and a lot of old nets in it.
Sela goes up. Obviously Sela goes up.
The nets have been moved recently. There's a clear patch about the size of a person lying down.
Somebody was sleeping up here, which is not quite the same thing.
Is there a back way out of this building?
A shutter at the gable end that opens onto the roof of the next one along.
social: Brannoc tries to get someone talking who isn't the man in charge.
There's a woman mending net by the long house who'll talk to you while she works.
How long has she lived here?
All her life, and her mother's life, and she says that like it's a complaint.
She stops mending for a second and then starts again and says the boats go out every spring and this year they didn't come back.
This year, plural? She said boats.
Does she seem frightened or does she seem resigned?
Sela asks a child instead. Children answer things.
A boy about nine says they're not allowed on the rise after dark any more, and he says it like it's very unfair.
Since three springs ago. He's very clear about it, because it's the same year he stopped being allowed.
Three springs ago keeps coming up.
Is anyone here armed? Do they have a watch, a militia, anything?
There are billhooks by most of the doors, and one of them has been sharpened this week.
One of them. Not all of them.
Brannoc asks whether there's anyone here who keeps the shrine.
She says there used to be, and that he's the reeve's uncle, and that he doesn't come down any more.
combat: Initiative. Everyone give me a number.
Nine, which is about right for Brannoc.
Sela, then them, then Tovald, then Brannoc. Sela, you're up.
Sela throws from cover. That's a fifteen to hit.
It goes in and it stays in and the thing does not care.
Tovald steps up and puts himself between it and Brannoc.
That's an attack of opportunity from the one on your flank. Eighteen against you.
Five, and you're grabbed. It's got your shield arm.
Brannoc moves up and puts light on the pair of them.
The one holding you flinches and the grip loosens but doesn't let go.
You're free and you're back a step. Their turn. Two of them come at the boat.
How much of the boat is left at this point?
Enough to float, not enough to be relaxed about.
Can I see how many are still coming?
More than you'd like and fewer than there were.
rules: speaker-3
Quick rules thing. Does the light count as an area or do I have to be in it?
speaker-1
It's an area, twenty feet, moves with Brannoc.
speaker-2
And it lasts how long? I want to know if I'm spending it now or holding it.
speaker-1
Ten minutes, and you've got two of them.
speaker-4
Does being in the water count as difficult terrain for the throwing?
speaker-1
Not for throwing. For moving, yes, half speed.
speaker-3
What about the shield? If I'm grabbed can I still use it?
speaker-1
Grabbed on the shield arm, so no, not this round.
speaker-2
Are we tracking rations properly or are we hand-waving it?
speaker-1
Track it while the village is cut off. Hand-wave it on the road.
speaker-4
Do I get advantage from cover on that or is it just the flat roll?
speaker-1
Flat roll, but they're at disadvantage against you while you're in the reeds.
speaker-3
Somebody write down that Tovald is at eleven, because I will forget.
speaker-2
Noted. Brannoc's full, Sela's full, Tovald's at eleven.
speaker-4
How much rope do we have after the trade? Actual number.
speaker-1
Forty feet new, plus whatever was left of the old, call it fifteen.
speaker-3
Fifty-five feet of rope and a river. That'll do.
speaker-2
Do we need light sources beyond Brannoc? Because I don't want to be the only light.
speaker-1
You've got the oil now, so lanterns are viable.
speaker-4
Sela takes a lantern and does not light it.
table: Sorry, can somebody pass the crisps.
There are none. There were none twenty minutes ago.
I'll go and put the kettle on in a minute, don't start anything important.
I'm going to start something important the second you leave the room, that's how this works.
Are we going two more hours or are we stopping at a decent point?
Let's see where we get to. I've got a good place to stop if we reach it.
Whose turn is it to write the recap for next time?
Mine, and I have not done the last one either.
Did anyone actually write down the name of the village?
It's Rackford. Or Wrackford. It's one of those.
It's Wrackford, with a W, and yes I know how it sounds.
Wrackford. Right. I've written Rackford in my notes twice.
Is anyone else's dice tower falling over or is it just mine.
It's just yours. It's been just yours for a year.
Can we get back to it, because the river is doing something.
Sorry, yes. Where were we, actually?
We were about to do something stupid, as usual.
You were about to do something reasonable that will turn out badly, which is different.
It is absolutely not a hint.
